label: People-Pleasing and the Fear of Man
framing: Scripture has an old, exact name for this: the fear of man, the dread of others' opinion that lays a snare for the feet. It is not the same as kindness; it is kindness hollowed out by fear, and the cure is not to care less for people but to fear God more, which strangely sets you free to love them.
cultural: We live in a world wired for the verdict of the crowd, where approval is counted in real time and the fear of being disliked has been turned into a business model. The result is a generation that confuses being liked with being loved and cannot tell its own convictions from the room's expectations. The Bible saw the snare long before the feed made it constant.
historical: Paul named the stakes plainly in his letter to the Galatians: if I were still trying to please man, I would not be a servant of Christ. The prophets before him paid for refusing the crowd, and Jeremiah was thrown in a cistern for it. Dietrich Bonhoeffer, writing in the nineteen-thirties under a regime that demanded the church's approval, called the fear of man a denial of the God who alone is to be feared, and he died refusing to flatter it.
application: Trace your yes back to its root and ask whether it comes from love or from fear of the no. Learn to say no kindly and without a paragraph of excuses, since the inability to disappoint anyone is not humility but bondage. Tell the truth even when it costs you approval, and let one relationship at a time be honest rather than smooth. The one whose face you are learning to seek already approves of you in Christ.

verses.text: The fear of man is a snare, but whoever trusts in the LORD is set securely on high.
verses.where: Near the close of the collection copied by Hezekiah's men, a proverb sets two fears side by side: the fear of man is a snare, but whoever trusts in the LORD is set securely on high. The site's note says trust in God frees a person from being controlled by others' approval. A snare is a trap a person walks into without seeing it, and the way out is not to care nothing for people but to lean on God more than on them.

verses.text: Then Saul said to Samuel, “I have sinned; I have transgressed the LORD’s commandment and your instructions, because I feared the people and obeyed their voice.
verses.where: Confronted by Samuel for not doing what the LORD had commanded, Saul first insists he obeyed and blames the troops. Then he says what was underneath: he feared the people and obeyed their voice. The note's summary turns on Samuel's answer that obedience is better than sacrifice. A king who could command an army could not bear the displeasure of the crowd, and it cost him his kingdom.

verses.text: Nevertheless, many of the leaders believed in Him; but because of the Pharisees they did not confess Him, for fear that they would be put out of the synagogue. For they loved praise from men more than praise from God.
verses.where: Many of the leaders in Jerusalem believed in Jesus but kept silent, afraid of being put out of the synagogue, the center of a town's prayer, friendships and help. John names the deeper cause: they loved praise from men more than praise from God. The site's plain note says these verses are not a verdict on the Jewish people, and that they are a mirror for every reader. It also notes that two such men, Nicodemus and Joseph of Arimathea, came into the open at Jesus' death.

verses.text: How can you believe if you accept glory from one another, yet do not seek the glory that comes from the only God?
verses.where: Jesus asks how people can believe while they accept glory from one another and do not seek the glory that comes from the only God. The site's plain note says the warning is for every religious person, Christians included: we too can prefer each other's praise to God's. Many people, it adds, hold back from Jesus not because of an argument but because of what the people around them would think.

verses.text: Am I now seeking the approval of men, or of God? Or am I striving to please men? If I were still trying to please men, I would not be a servant of Christ.
verses.where: Some in Galatia said Paul made the gospel easy so that Gentiles would like him. Paul answers with a question: is he seeking the approval of men, or of God? The site's plain note says a man who has just written what Paul wrote is plainly not trying to be popular. If he were still trying to please people, he says, he would not be a servant of Christ.

verses.text: When Cephas came to Antioch, however, I opposed him to his face, because he stood to be condemned. For before certain men came from James, he used to eat with the Gentiles. But when they arrived, he began to draw back and separate himself, for fear of those in the circumcision group.
verses.where: Peter had been eating with Gentile believers in Antioch, but when certain men came from James he drew back, for fear of those in the circumcision group. The site's plain note calls it a moment of fear in a good man, under real pressure, trying perhaps to keep faith with people on both sides: his actions did not match what he believed. Paul opposed him openly, and the friendship did not end there.

verses.text: “I, even I, am He who comforts you. Why should you be afraid of mortal man, of a son of man who withers like grass?
verses.where: God speaks to exiles who live in fear of an oppressor, as the site's note on the chapter describes them, and he answers their fear with comfort: he is the one who comforts them, so why should they be afraid of a mortal who withers like grass? The people who frighten us are real, and they are also mortal. The God who made the heavens is neither.

verses.text: For our appeal does not arise from deceit or ulterior motives or trickery. Instead, we speak as those approved by God to be entrusted with the gospel, not in order to please men but God, who examines our hearts.
verses.where: Paul reminds the Thessalonians how he preached among them, not from deceit, greed or a wish for praise, but as one entrusted with the gospel, speaking to please God, who examines the heart. The site's plain note asks whose approval a reader most wants, and where flattery has crept into their words at work, at church or at home. The same chapter says Paul was gentle among them like a nursing mother; refusing to flatter did not make him cold.

verses.text: “Be careful not to perform your righteous acts before men to be seen by them. If you do, you will have no reward from your Father in heaven.
verses.where: Jesus warns against doing good in order to be seen. The site's note says even real righteousness can be spoiled by the wish for an audience, and the plain note adds that Jesus is not offering payment for good deeds: the Father notices what no one else sees, and his well done is worth more than the crowd's. A life lived for applause can be full of good acts and still be hollow at the center.

verses.text: Woe to you when all men speak well of you, for their fathers treated the false prophets in the same way.
verses.where: The last of Jesus' woes in Luke answers the last of his blessings: woe when everyone speaks well of you, because that is how the ancestors treated the false prophets. The site's note puts it plainly: universal praise is a warning sign. A person who is never disagreed with may have stopped saying anything true.

verses.text: The wounds of a friend are faithful, but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful.
verses.where: The wounds of a friend are faithful, the proverb says, but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful. The site's note on the chapter gathers its sayings on the value of honest friends and honest rebuke. The one who only ever tells people what they want to hear is not being kind to them.

links.label: Practical guides for the inner life

misread.taken: Paul's words that he tries to please everyone in all he does are sometimes taken as the Christian way of life: keep everyone happy, never disappoint anyone, and treat any displeasure as a failure of love.
misread.says: The site's plain note on the passage sets the verse in its argument about food offered to idols: Paul gives up his own freedom when someone else's faith is at stake, not seeking his own good, but the good of many, that they may be saved. His aim is their good, not their approval. The same Paul wrote that if he were still trying to please people he would not be a servant of Christ, and he opposed Peter to his face in Antioch. Pleasing others for their good sometimes means disappointing them.
misread.text: Do not become a stumbling block, whether to Jews or Greeks or the church of God— as I also try to please everyone in all I do. For I am not seeking my own good, but the good of many, that they may be saved.

misread.taken: Live at peace with everyone is used to mean that a Christian should avoid every conflict, never say no, and keep the peace at any cost, even with someone who is hurting them.
misread.says: Paul adds two conditions: if it is possible, and on your part. The site's plain note on the chapter says that blessing an enemy and leaving vengeance to God does not mean staying in danger or keeping silent about harm. A peace kept by never telling the truth is not the peace Paul means, and a person answers for their own part of it, not for how everyone else feels.
misread.text: If it is possible on your part, live at peace with everyone.

whole: Most people who live to please others would not call it fear. They call it being easygoing, or helpful, or kind. They say yes to the committee, the extra shift, the relative who always needs money, because a no feels unbearable. They rehearse conversations to make sure no one could be upset. They agree in the room and disagree in the car. They notice every flicker of disapproval on a face and spend the evening replaying it. Over time they lose track of what they themselves think, because their opinions have been shaped for so long by what will keep the peace. It is exhausting, and it can look so much like love that the person living it is the last to see what it costs.

Scripture has an old and exact name for it: the fear of man. Proverbs calls it a snare. Saul, who could command an army, disobeyed God because he feared the people and obeyed their voice. Leaders in Jerusalem believed in Jesus and kept silent because they loved praise from men more than praise from God. Even Peter, who had walked with Jesus, drew back from Gentile believers in Antioch for fear of what one group would think. The Bible does not tell these stories to sneer at weak people. It tells them because the fear is so common, and because it grows in good people, in leaders, and in the church. Most of us have shaded the truth to stay liked, or kept quiet when speaking would have cost us. Underneath it there is often a hunger to be approved by someone, and a fear that without that approval we are nothing.

So the Bible's answer is not to care less about people. Paul, who refused to please men, was gentle among the Thessalonians like a nursing mother, and he gave up his own freedom for the good of others. The answer is to fear God more, and to find in him the approval that no crowd can give or take away. Jesus says the Father sees what no one else sees, and his well done is worth more than the applause. In practice that may mean saying a plain no without a long excuse, giving an honest opinion when it is asked for, letting someone be disappointed without rushing to fix it, and telling a friend a hard truth because you love them. It may mean asking, before a yes, whose approval you are reaching for. Where pleasing someone has become fear of what they will do to you, that is a different matter: no verse asks anyone to stay in danger to keep the peace, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

The hope Scripture gives is that the approval people chase is already given to those who are in Christ. God does not love his children because they keep everyone happy, and he will not stop loving them when someone frowns. The people who frighten us are real, Isaiah says, and they wither like grass; God, who comforts his people, does not. Peter, who drew back at Antioch, was not cast off; he was corrected and went on. The fear of man loosens slowly, as a person learns again and again that the one whose opinion matters most has already spoken. The LORD is on my side, the psalm says; I will not be afraid. What can man do to me?
deep.sit: Whose disappointment are you most afraid of right now, and what would you say or do this week if you believed that God's approval of you was already settled?

prayer.lead: A song of someone surrounded and afraid who sets God's help against the power of people. The site's plain note says its brave question does not mean nothing bad can happen; it means people do not have the last word over someone God holds.
prayer.text: The LORD is on my side; I will not be afraid. What can man do to me? The LORD is on my side; He is my helper. Therefore I will look in triumph on those who hate me. It is better to take refuge in the LORD than to trust in man. It is better to take refuge in the LORD than to trust in princes.

careLines.text: Nothing in this passage asks anyone to stay where they or their children are in danger.
The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
